open_obligations: Note the different settings: chess, NLP and reward modeling versus Yang et al.'s deception experiments with Mistral-7B as the strong model.
Check whether Yang et al.'s gains are on the same metric (PGR) as Burns et al.'s.
Check consistency with Burns et al.'s finding of no improvement in reward modeling.
out.other_title: Bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves weak-to-strong PGR on chess
out.rationale: Burns et al. report bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves PGR on chess puzzles, with only small gains on NLP tasks and none in the reward modeling setting in preliminary experiments. Yang et al. report that when the weak model supervises an intermediate model that then supervises Mistral-7B, generalization performance can improve and deception scores are consistently lower. Both ask whether supervising through an intermediate model helps, but in different settings: Yang et al. study weak-to-strong deception with Mistral-7B as the strong model, while Burns et al.'s positive result is on chess and they saw no improvement in the reward modeling setting.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether supervising through an intermediate model improves weak-to-strong generalization

text: The paper reports that when the weak model first supervises an intermediate model that then supervises Mistral-7B, bootstrapping improves weak-to-strong generalization (consistent with Burns et al.) and consistently lowers deception scores. The authors suggest some cases unknown to the weak model become known to the intermediate model, making deception harder there.
title: Bootstrapping through an intermediate model partly mitigates weak-to-strong deception
